identification: Tall annual grass with loose, drooping panicles. Leaves are broad and flat with a ligule. Grows 30-120 cm tall. Seeds have long awns and are easily scattered by wind.
symptomsOrImpact: Competes aggressively with wheat for nutrients, water, and sunlight. Reduces tillering and grain filling in wheat.
yieldImpact: Can reduce wheat yield by 20-50% in heavy infestations.
pestHosting: Can host aphids and cereal cyst nematodes that also affect wheat.
controlPeriod: Pre-emergence to early post-emergence (first 4-6 weeks after sowing).
culturalControl: Use certified clean seed. Practice crop rotation with non-cereal crops. Maintain optimal sowing density to suppress weed growth.
mechanicalControl: Hand weeding or hoeing before flowering. Deep ploughing before sowing to bury weed seeds.
chemicalControl: Pre-emergence or early post-emergence herbicide application may be used. Consult local agricultural extension services for approved products and application timing specific to your region.
prevention: Use clean seed free from weed contamination. Rotate crops regularly. Clean farm machinery between fields to prevent seed transfer.

identification: Erect annual grass growing 30-100 cm. Dense cylindrical spike-like panicle. Bluish-green leaves with a prominent membranous ligule.
symptomsOrImpact: Strong competitor in irrigated wheat fields. Reduces light availability and competes for soil nutrients.
yieldImpact: Can cause 20-40% yield loss in severe infestations.
pestHosting: May host rust pathogens and aphids.
controlPeriod: Early growth stage of wheat (2-4 leaf stage of weed).
culturalControl: Avoid late sowing of wheat. Maintain proper irrigation scheduling. Use competitive wheat varieties.
mechanicalControl: Hand weeding at 3-4 weeks after sowing. Rogue out before seed set.
chemicalControl: Herbicide application at early post-emergence stage. Always follow label instructions and consult local agricultural experts for region-specific recommendations.
prevention: Prevent seed set by controlling before flowering. Clean harvest equipment. Use weed-free seed.

identification: Coarse annual grass, 30-150 cm tall. Purplish tinge at the base. Panicle has dense, bristly spikelets. No ligule in the leaf collar region.
symptomsOrImpact: One of the most competitive weeds in rice paddies. Absorbs large quantities of nitrogen from the soil.
yieldImpact: Can reduce rice yield by 25-50% depending on density and duration of competition.
pestHosting: Hosts rice stem borers and leaf hoppers.
controlPeriod: Within the first 30 days after transplanting or seeding.
culturalControl: Maintain standing water of 5-10 cm in paddy fields. Use well-decomposed organic matter. Practice proper land leveling.
mechanicalControl: Hand weeding at 15 and 30 days after transplanting. Use rotary weeders in transplanted rice.
chemicalControl: Pre-emergence and early post-emergence herbicide options exist. Consult with local extension officers for appropriate products for rice paddies.
prevention: Use clean nursery seedlings. Maintain proper water management. Prevent weed seed entry through irrigation water.

identification: Closely resembles cultivated rice but has red or reddish-brown bran. Shatters seeds easily at maturity. Often taller than the cultivated variety with more tillers.
symptomsOrImpact: Competes directly with cultivated rice since it is the same species. Reduces grain quality when mixed in harvest.
yieldImpact: Can cause 15-30% yield loss and significantly reduces milling quality.
pestHosting: Shares the same pests and diseases as cultivated rice.
controlPeriod: Critical period is first 45 days after sowing.
culturalControl: Use certified seed free of red rice. Practice crop rotation with non-rice crops. Stale seedbed technique before planting.
mechanicalControl: Hand rogue before panicle emergence. Remove red rice plants that are taller than the crop.
chemicalControl: Limited chemical options since it is the same species as rice. Consult agricultural extension services for integrated management strategies.
prevention: Use certified clean seed. Avoid direct seeding in fields with known red rice history. Rotate with upland crops.

identification: Perennial sedge with triangular stem, 15-60 cm tall. Dark green leaves arranged in three rows. Produces chains of small tubers (nutlets) underground.
symptomsOrImpact: One of the world's worst weeds. Tubers release allelopathic chemicals that inhibit crop growth. Penetrates plastic mulch.
yieldImpact: Can reduce cotton yield by 30-80% in heavy infestations.
pestHosting: Hosts root-knot nematodes and several insect pests.
controlPeriod: Year-round management needed. Critical during crop establishment phase.
culturalControl: Deep summer ploughing to expose tubers to sun. Crop rotation with competitive crops like sorghum. Use thick organic mulch.
mechanicalControl: Repeated hoeing at 2-3 week intervals to exhaust tuber reserves. Hand pulling is ineffective as tubers remain in soil.
chemicalControl: Systemic herbicides may provide some control. Repeated applications are usually necessary. Consult local agricultural authorities for registered products.
prevention: Prevent tuber spread through irrigation water and farm machinery. Inspect and clean equipment between fields.

identification: Prostrate succulent annual herb. Reddish stems spreading on ground. Small yellow flowers. Fleshy leaves. Can root from stem fragments.
symptomsOrImpact: Competes for water and nutrients. Can survive in dry conditions due to succulent nature. Interferes with cotton picking.
yieldImpact: Moderate yield loss of 10-25% in heavy infestations.
pestHosting: May host aphids and whiteflies that also affect cotton.
controlPeriod: Early growth stages of the crop.
culturalControl: Maintain good crop canopy. Use competitive crop varieties with early canopy closure.
mechanicalControl: Hand weeding before flowering. Hoeing at regular intervals during early crop growth.
chemicalControl: Pre-emergence herbicides can provide early control. Consult local agricultural advisory services for current recommendations.
prevention: Remove plants before seed set. Prevent spread through contaminated soil or irrigation water.

identification: Tall perennial grass, 50-200 cm. Sharp-edged leaves with prominent white midrib. Extensive rhizome system underground. Silky white seed heads.
symptomsOrImpact: Highly invasive with deep rhizome system. Strong allelopathic effect on neighboring crops. Difficult to eradicate once established.
yieldImpact: Can reduce sugarcane yield by 25-55% in heavily infested fields.
pestHosting: Hosts sugarcane mosaic virus and several insect pests.
controlPeriod: Pre-planting and early crop growth stages.
culturalControl: Deep ploughing and repeated cultivation to exhaust rhizome reserves. Flooding for extended periods can suppress growth.
mechanicalControl: Deep digging to remove rhizomes before planting. Regular cutting during crop growth to prevent shading.
chemicalControl: Systemic herbicides applied pre-planting or as directed spray may help. Multiple applications typically needed. Always consult local agricultural services.
prevention: Prevent rhizome spread through contaminated soil. Maintain field boundaries. Monitor and treat early infestations.

identification: Creeping perennial grass with both above-ground stolons and below-ground rhizomes. Short flat leaves. Finger-like seed heads. Forms dense mats.
symptomsOrImpact: Competes vigorously for water, nutrients, and light. Spreads rapidly through stolons and rhizomes. Interferes with crop management operations.
pestHosting: Hosts various insects including armyworms and leafhoppers.
controlPeriod: Pre-planting and first 60 days of crop growth.
culturalControl: Solarization of soil before planting. Use well-decomposed manure. Maintain crop vigor for competitive advantage.
mechanicalControl: Deep ploughing followed by repeated harrowing to destroy rhizomes and stolons.
chemicalControl: Pre-emergence herbicides or directed post-emergence application. Follow label rates and consult local agricultural advisory services.
prevention: Clean irrigation channels. Prevent stolon entry from adjacent areas. Maintain field boundaries.

identification: Prostrate annual herb with paired leaves. Small yellow flowers. Spiny hard fruit (burrs) that puncture tires and injure feet. Grows 15-60 cm.
symptomsOrImpact: Competes for moisture and nutrients. Spiny fruits interfere with harvesting operations and can injure workers and livestock.
yieldImpact: Can cause 10-30% yield reduction in maize.
controlPeriod: Pre-emergence to early growth stage of the crop.
culturalControl: Maintain competitive crop stand. Avoid over-irrigation which promotes weed growth.
mechanicalControl: Hand weeding or hoeing before flowering. Remove and destroy plants before fruit formation.
chemicalControl: Pre-emergence herbicides can provide early season control. Consult local agricultural extension for approved options.
prevention: Remove plants before burrs form. Prevent livestock from carrying burrs into clean fields. Clean farm equipment.

identification: Semi-parasitic plant, 15-60 cm tall. Bright purple or white flowers. Small narrow leaves. Attaches to host roots underground.
symptomsOrImpact: Parasitic weed that attaches to crop roots and extracts water and nutrients. Causes wilting, stunting, and yellowing even with adequate soil moisture.
yieldImpact: Can cause 30-70% yield loss in severe infestations.
pestHosting: Not a significant pest host, but weakens the crop making it more susceptible to other pests.
culturalControl: Use Striga-resistant crop varieties where available. Intercrop with legumes like cowpea. Practice trap cropping.
mechanicalControl: Hand pull before seed set to reduce seed bank. Do not allow Striga to flower.
chemicalControl: Limited chemical options. Some seed treatment herbicides show promise. Consult research institutions for latest recommendations.
prevention: Use clean seed. Prevent seed spread. Rotate with non-host crops like legumes for several seasons.

identification: Low-growing annual legume with trifoliate leaves. Small yellow flowers. Coiled spiny seed pods. Grows 10-50 cm.
symptomsOrImpact: Competes for light and moisture in chickpea fields. Can make harvesting difficult when tangled with the crop.
pestHosting: May host aphids and pod borers.
culturalControl: Use competitive chickpea varieties. Maintain narrow row spacing for early canopy closure.
mechanicalControl: Hand weeding at 25-30 days after sowing. One or two weedings usually sufficient.
chemicalControl: Pre-emergence herbicide application may help. Consult local agricultural services for registered products for chickpea.
prevention: Use clean seed. Rotate with cereal crops. Maintain good field sanitation.

identification: Prostrate annual or biennial herb. Small white flowers. Pungent smell when crushed. Finely divided leaves. Grows 5-30 cm.
symptomsOrImpact: Competes with low-growing crops. Taints grain if harvested together. Strong odor can contaminate crop produce.
yieldImpact: Can cause 10-20% yield loss in chickpea.
pestHosting: Generally not a significant pest host.
culturalControl: Timely sowing at recommended dates. Proper seed rate for competitive crop stand.
mechanicalControl: Hand weeding at early growth stage before flowering.
chemicalControl: Broadleaf herbicides may be effective. Follow local agricultural advisory for proper product selection.
prevention: Clean seed and prevent seed contamination during harvest.

identification: Erect annual herb, 30-120 cm. White star-shaped flowers. Deeply lobed leaves. Spreads prolifically through tiny seeds. Strong allergenic properties.
symptomsOrImpact: Allelopathic weed that inhibits growth of nearby plants. Competes for water and nutrients in orchards. Can cause contact dermatitis in workers.
yieldImpact: Can reduce mango yield by 10-25% through competition and allelopathic effects.
pestHosting: Hosts fruit flies and mealybugs that attack mango.
culturalControl: Maintain cover crops in orchard alleys. Use mulch around tree bases. Regular mowing of orchard floor.
mechanicalControl: Uprooting before flowering. Regular slashing of orchard floor vegetation. Hand pulling for small infestations.
chemicalControl: Contact and systemic herbicides may be used in orchard alleys away from tree trunks. Follow local regulations and consult agricultural authorities.
prevention: Prevent seed set and spread. Biological control agents (Zygogramma beetle) are available in some regions. Maintain competitive ground cover.

identification: Twining vine with heart-shaped leaves. Trumpet-shaped flowers in purple, pink, or white. Can climb over crop plants. Extensive root system.
symptomsOrImpact: Climbs over young mango trees and can smother them. Competes for light and can break young branches with its weight.
yieldImpact: Can reduce young orchard establishment success by 20-35%. Less impact on mature trees.
pestHosting: May host whiteflies, aphids, and fungal pathogens.
controlPeriod: Year-round, especially during rainy season when growth is vigorous.
culturalControl: Maintain clean orchard floor with regular maintenance. Use cover crops that outcompete morning glory.
mechanicalControl: Cut vines at ground level and remove from orchard. Dig out root systems where possible.
chemicalControl: Systemic herbicides applied carefully to avoid crop contact. Consult agricultural extension for orchard-safe products.
prevention: Prevent vine from flowering and setting seed. Regular orchard floor maintenance. Monitor boundaries.

identification: Erect annual herb, 30-80 cm. Small white or purple flowers. Black or green berries. Oval leaves with wavy margins. Same family as potato.
symptomsOrImpact: Competes for nutrients, water, and light. Can harbor diseases common to potato including late blight. Berries contaminate harvest.
yieldImpact: Can reduce potato yield by 15-35% in heavy infestations.
pestHosting: Hosts late blight (Phytophthora), Colorado potato beetle, and aphids.
controlPeriod: Pre-emergence and early growth stages of potato.
culturalControl: Use competitive potato varieties. Proper hilling to bury small weeds. Maintain crop vigor.
mechanicalControl: Hand weeding before flowering. Mechanical cultivation between rows before canopy closure.
chemicalControl: Pre-emergence herbicides are commonly used in potato. Follow local agricultural advisory for approved products.
prevention: Remove plants before fruiting. Prevent contamination of potato seed stock. Rotate with non-solanaceous crops.

identification: Small annual herb, 10-30 cm. Square stem. Pink to purple tubular flowers in whorls at stem tips. Rounded leaves clasping the stem.
symptomsOrImpact: Competes with young potato plants for moisture and nutrients. Can interfere with mechanical harvesting.
yieldImpact: Can cause 5-15% yield reduction in potato.
pestHosting: May host aphids and serve as alternate host for some viral diseases.
controlPeriod: Pre-emergence and early crop growth stages.
culturalControl: Maintain competitive crop. Proper planting density and fertilization.
mechanicalControl: Hand weeding or mechanical cultivation before crop canopy closure.
chemicalControl: Broadleaf herbicides can be effective. Follow local registration and application guidelines.
prevention: Prevent seed production. Clean field equipment. Rotate crops.
